content: Growth retardation is a frequent complication observed in children with chronic kidney disease (CKD), which can be a significant concern for their families. Recombinant human growth hormone (rhGH) therapy has been utilized to help children with CKD who are shorter than their peers achieve a height closer to that of their age group. However, there are ongoing concerns regarding the long-term efficacy of rhGH in significantly improving final adult height. Additionally, there are potential adverse effects associated with rhGH therapy, including worsening of native kidney function, an increased risk of acute rejection in kidney transplant recipients, and the development of benign intracranial hypertension. The objective of this study was to assess both the benefits and potential harms of rhGH treatment in children diagnosed with CKD. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) were identified through a comprehensive search of multiple databases, including the Cochrane Renal Group's Specialised Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, and EMBASE, as well as through reference lists of relevant articles and consultation with experts in the field. The search was last updated on December 29, 2011. The inclusion criteria for the RCTs were as follows: studies involving children aged 0 to 18 years diagnosed with CKD, whether pre-dialysis, on dialysis, or post-transplant; studies comparing rhGH treatment with either placebo, no treatment, or different doses of rhGH; and studies reporting height-related outcomes. Two independent authors assessed the risk of bias in the studies and extracted data. A random-effects model was used to pool the data, and mean differences (MD) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) were calculated for continuous outcomes. A total of 16 studies involving 809 children were included in the analysis. The risk of bias was generally high, with only four studies adequately reporting allocation concealment and five studies reporting blinding of participants and investigators. Treatment with rhGH at a dose of 28 IU/m² per week, compared to placebo or no specific therapy, resulted in a significant improvement in height standard deviation score (HSDS) after one year (8 studies, 391 children: MD 0.82, 95% CI 0.56 to 1.07). Additionally, there was a significant increase in height velocity at six months (2 studies, 27 children: MD 2.85 cm/6 months, 95% CI 2.22 to 3.48) and at one year (7 studies, 287 children: MD 3.88 cm/year, 95% CI 3.32 to 4.44). Although the height velocity decreased during the second year of therapy, it remained significantly higher than in untreated children (1 study, 82 children: MD 2.30 cm/year, 95% CI 1.39 to 3.21). When comparing two doses of rhGH, the 28 IU/m² per week group demonstrated a 1.18 cm/year greater increase in height velocity compared to the 14 IU/m² per week group (3 studies, 150 children: MD 1.18 cm/year, 95% CI 0.52 to 1.84). The frequency of adverse effects reported in children receiving rhGH therapy was generally similar to that observed in the control group. In conclusion, one year of rhGH therapy at a dose of 28 IU/m² per week in children with CKD resulted in a 3.88 cm/year increase in height velocity compared to untreated patients. However, the studies included in this analysis were of insufficient duration to determine whether continued treatment with rhGH leads to an increase in final adult height.
